meta.title: Generalized Hawking-Page transitions
meta.abstractHtml: We construct holographic backgrounds that are dual by the AdS/CFT correspondence to Euclidean conformal field theories on products of spheres , for conformal field theories whose dual may be approximated by classical Einstein gravity (typically these are large strongly coupled theories). For these backgrounds correspond to thermal field theories on , and Hawking and Page found that there are several possible bulk solutions, with two different topologies, that compete with each other, leading to a phase transition as the relative size of the spheres is modified. By numerically solving the Einstein equations we find similar results also for , with bulk solutions in which either one or the other sphere shrinks to zero smoothly at a minimal value of the radial coordinate, and with a first order phase transition (for ) between solutions of two different topologies as the relative radius changes. For a critical ratio of the radii there is a (sub-dominant) singular solution where both spheres shrink, and we analytically analyze the behavior near this radius. For the number of solutions grows to infinity as the critical ratio is approached.

children.body: Gauge/gravity duality allows us to translate results in gravity to results in field theory, and vice versa. In particular, there is a large set of examples of -dimensional conformal field theories (CFTs) whose dual is well-approximated by classical Einstein gravity on (times some compact manifold). These include the large supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory at strong ‘t Hooft coupling, and the large maximally supersymmetric and CFTs. For these theories classical computations in gravity can teach us about the behavior of the field theory (in the large limit). Moreover, since the gravitational sector is shared between many different field theories (which differ, for instance, in the choice of compact manifold), gravity computations give us universal results that are valid for many different field theories.

CFTs on some manifold are dual by the AdS/CFT correspondence to gravitational theories on asymptotically anti-de Sitter (AdS) spaces, whose boundary is conformally equivalent to . The most studied examples are or , where the metric is exactly anti-de Sitter. Not many results are known about other spaces (see, for instance, [1, 2, 3] for some general comments). One particularly interesting example is the Euclidean space , first studied by Hawking and Page [4]. This is interesting because it corresponds to the CFT on at finite temperature. Hawking and Page showed that there are two classes of smooth solutions with these boundary conditions. One set of solutions is given by anti-de Sitter space in global coordinates with Euclidean time identified; in this solution the factor shrinks to zero in the interior of space, such that the topology is . The other set is described by Euclidean black holes, in which the shrinks to zero in the interior at the Euclidean horizon; this set has the topology . The AdS/CFT correspondence identifies the partition function of the Euclidean field theory, in the gravity approximation, with the exponent of minus the Euclidean gravitational action (summed over all solutions with given boundary conditions). Hawking and Page showed that different classical solutions dominate the partition function at different temperatures (different ratios of the radius to the radius), with a phase transition between them at some critical temperature. When the dual field theory is a gauge theory, this phase transition may be identified (using various order parameters) with a confinement/deconfinement transition [5, 6]. On the field theory side, a sharp phase transition at finite volume is possible only when the number of degrees of freedom is infinite; for a finite number we expect a crossover. The translation of this to the gravity side is that quantum effects (corresponding to corrections in the field theory) will turn the phase transition into a crossover.

In this paper we generalize the discussion of Hawking and Page to CFTs on . This no longer has a thermal interpretation, but the CFT partition function on such Euclidean manifolds is still an interesting observable. Similar observables are computed analytically using localization in supersymmetric CFTs [7]. The result may also be related by analytic continuation to the physics of the canonical vacuum state in the CFT on the -dimensional de Sitter space times  [8]. For this case we also find that there are two possible topologies, and , and that there is a phase transition between them as the ratio of radii, is varied. We were not able to find analytical solutions for general , but we find numerical solutions for various values of ; the large isometry group of the space implies that the equations of motion are ordinary differential equations in a single variable. One important difference from the case is that here only one solution exists for and for ; there is no analog of the thermal AdS solution that exists for all ratios. In addition, there is in this case a solution with a conical singularity where both spheres shrink together, for some critical ratio . This solution can be found analytically, and we can also analyze analytically the small fluctuations around it. For we find oscillatory behavior of these fluctuations, such that the number of solutions with a given ratio grows as ; however, the new solutions and the singular solution never dominate, and there is a first order phase transition between the solution which exists at and the solution (of the other topology) which exists at , at some critical close to . The case of is unphysical, since there are no consistent quantum gravitational theories that have such solution with small curvature (indeed, even without requiring a gravity dual, there are so far no known interacting conformal field theories with ). However, the classical analysis can be performed also in this case, and leads to a second order phase transition at , with only one solution existing for every value of .

The phase structure of the Hawking-Page case, and of the case with , are schematically summarized in figure 1. The case of a CFT on was already studied by the same methods in [8], with the motivation of continuing the sphere to de Sitter space, and understanding thermal phase transitions in de Sitter space for confining theories arising from CFTs on . The results we find for the phase structure exactly agree with theirs. As in the case of the Hawking-Page transition, quantum effects should turn the phase transition into a crossover, bu we do not discuss them here.

We begin in section 2 by describing the setup and the observables we can compute. In section 3 we discuss in detail the singular solution and the perturbations around it. In section 4 we present some details of our numerical implementation of the holographic renormalization which is needed for computing the Euclidean action. Our numerical results are presented in section 5 for the specific case of , and then in section 6 we briefly present the results for some other representative examples.

The topology of space is different on the two sides of the phase transition, but in the pure gravity theory there is no simple order parameter that distinguishes them. If our bulk gravity theory contains -dimensional extended objects which can end on the boundary, then these correspond to -dimensional extended operators in the CFT; for example, this happens for when we have a string theory in the bulk, and strings ending on the boundary may be identified with Wilson loops. In such a case, the expectation value of the -dimensional operator integrated on gives an order parameter for the phase transition, since one can find -dimensional extended configurations in the bulk that end on the , leading to a non-zero expectation value, if and only if the topology is of the form . A similar discussion applies with . In many examples of the AdS/CFT correspondence such order parameters exist, but their field theory interpretation depends on the specific case, and we will not discuss it here.

children.body: Our results give a universal behavior for all theories that are well-approximated by classical Einstein gravity in some limit. We consider solutions where only the gravitational field is turned on, and no other fields. Assuming that all other fields are set to zero at the boundary, it is natural to expect that they will vanish in the minimal-action solutions, but this may not be true in some examples, in which case our solutions would be sub-leading saddle points in these examples.

In many cases it is interesting to turn on additional bulk fields in addition to the metric. In particular, for supersymmetric theories, it is often interesting to compactify them on in a way that preserves supersymmetry, and this requires turning on additional fields. In this paper we discuss only solutions with no extra fields; in particular in supersymmetric theories, these solutions preserve no supersymmetry (since it is broken by the compactification of the field theory on , in the absence of extra background fields). It would be interesting to look for solutions in which extra fields are turned on. There are also many other generalizations of our work, to different space-times, with products of more spheres, or with smaller isometry groups.

It would also be interesting to investigate other field theories, that do not have a dual described by classical Einstein gravity. These can include weakly coupled field theories, whose partition function can be computed in perturbation theory, and it would be interesting to compare their qualitative behavior to the one that we find here for strongly coupled field theories (for the case, a similar transition exists at large also in weakly coupled gauge theories [9, 10]).

Our goal is to find Euclidean gravitational duals of CFTs on the space , for -dimensional CFTs () whose holographic dual is well-approximated by classical Einstein gravity on (perhaps multiplied by some compact space, which we assume nothing depends on so that it will play no role in our discussion). Namely, we look for -dimensional manifolds that satisfy the (Euclidean) Einstein equations with a negative cosmological constant , and have a conformal boundary . We assume for simplicity that no additional fields are turned on except the metric; this gives us universal solutions that are present in all CFTs of this type, though they may not necessarily be the dominant solutions for specific CFTs. We will also assume the manifolds preserve the symmetries of the space that the CFT lives on1, and can thus can be foliated into orbits. We can therefore write the metric as

Here we chose a convenient reparameterization of the radial coordinate , with the boundary at , and space ending smoothly at in the interior. The cosmological constant dictates the asymptotic behavior as , where is related to the AdS radius; we will work in units with from here on. The range of is infinite; for our numerics it will be useful to work with a different coordinate that will have a finite range in our solutions. In terms of this coordinate we write:

At the beginning we use mostly the convention. Starting from the end of section 3 we switch to the convention to calculate asymptotic observables.

In order to find the phase diagram of the theory we need to find all the saddle-point metrics with the same asymptotic geometry . We can label the solution by the triad . This label is not unique since several solutions (corresponding to different ’s) might have the same asymptotic . In general we need to sum the contributions to from different saddle points; in the large limit the actions are very large so we can ignore any subleading saddle points. Given an asymptotic geometry, the free energy (defined as minus the log of the partition function) is the minimum between the actions of all the different configurations with either or . We denote this function by , and it encodes the different phases of the CFT. In the case of , after dividing by , this quantity is just the thermal free energy as a function of the inverse temperature.

children.body: Some qualitative properties of the phase diagram are apparent without calculation. In the limit , where at the boundary, we expect the smaller sphere to shrink much before the larger one, such that the only solution would have the topology with a large .3 We also expect the CFT on such a space to behave like some -dimensional theory on , which is obtained by KK reduction on the other sphere. Thus, to first order the action should scale like the normalized volume of , which is . Symmetrically, for the solution will be topologically with a large , and the action will scale like . So for both the action diverges, each limit as a result of a different bulk topology. Consequently, at least one phase transition is expected between the two topologies. Naively one may expect that decreasing decreases the asymptotic radius of the corresponding sphere, until some critical radius where , where this branch of solutions connects to the branch with the other topology. In this case there would be just a single solution for every radius in the CFT, and a smooth transition between the two branches at . We will see that this is true when , but not in the physically interesting range of dimensions , where the asymptotic radius will not be monotonic in . In this range more than one solution of the same topology can exist for the same asymptotic radii. Recall that this happens already for , where both “large” and “small” AdS black holes can exist with the same temperature.

From the analysis above we can draw a schematic picture of the phase map (figure 1). Around the action diverges like respectively (we take ), each divergence comes from a different bulk topology. The two branches coincide at and at the same action. From (3.10) we expect decayed oscillations of toward as . Because (3.14), the two topologies approach in with zero slope. We now label the CFT geometry by the ratio of the radius to the radius, where . Note that in the notations of section 2 we need to consider solutions both with a closed sphere and ratio , and with a closed sphere and ratio . children.body: The analytical examination above (section 3) suggests that for large the open sphere in the IR would stay bigger along the bulk, and the final ratio of radii would be very large or very small (depending on the convention for the ratio). For small a complex critical exponent was predicted near (3.3). In figure 2 we can see exactly those characteristics. Similar behavior can be found also for other (see section 6). The analytical description captures all the qualitative features appearing in the figures.

The behavior of around the singular solution was found above to take the form where and . In order to check this result we fitted the log of the calculated to the aforementioned equation, to find . The fit was taken with the function FindFit of Mathematica with 100 data points, for between and (which is also the lower bound for accurate results of using the Mathematica integrator). The results are presented in table 1. The numerical exponent agrees with the analytical one to high precision. It is evident that the error in the fit grows with the total dimension . This is because the frequency becomes smaller as gets closer to , making it more difficult to estimate it over the same data range. As expected, no oscillations were found for (not shown in the table).

children.body: In figure 1 we drew a schematic picture of , the action as a function of the ratio. We expect to diverge. We also expect the two topologies to approach with zero-slope decayed oscillations. In all cases, we found numerically that the action decreases at second order in the expansion around the singular solution. We haven’t found an analytical explanation for this fact. Thus the simplest scenario (like the one drawn in figure 1) would be a single first order phase transition between the two topologies, close to . Figure 3 agrees with this description and exhibits one first order phase transition. The critical ratio of the phase transition for this case agree with the results previously found in [8].

There are two cases that display a somewhat different behavior than that in figures 1 and 3. The first is the case of equal spheres . The behavior there is very similar besides the sign of the divergence at (we show examples of this in the next section). The second is the Hawking-Page , shown on the left-hand side of figure 1, where there are no oscillations (as there is no singular solution).

The only difference is the sign of the coefficient of in the action for . As the two limits are identical, the sign is symmetric, but it depends on . Figures 11, 12 and 13 give the ratio of radii, the action and the stress tensor of the theory, respectively. The qualitative discussion in section 5 is relevant to this case as well. Our results for the phase structure in this case agree with the results previously found in [8].

  4. 4
    In this paper we assume that the higher curvature corrections to Einstein’s equations are small, and we neglect them. This will not be true when both and are very small, so our solutions cannot be trusted there. The features of the solutions that we describe will be independent of the form of these corrections for . For , where the singular solution is dominant for some value of , the corrections will be important in order to determine the precise nature of the phase transition; however, this case is unphysical.
